newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Spain aims to join EMU starting group - Aznar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain aims to join EMU starting group - Aznar.

text.p: Spanish prime minister Jose Maria Aznar said his country was intent on meeting the requirements for European monetary union (EMU) this year, putting it in the starting group of countries.
Aznar said Spain will slash its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year, the target set by the Maastricht Treaty for participation in the single currency.

In an interview with the weekly Die Zeit, Aznar said, "Our budget for 1997 is the most stringent in 20 years. We will reach without problems the Maastricht goal of shrinking the deficit to three percent of GDP."

A copy of the interview was made available by Die Zeit ahead of its scheduled publication on Thursday. Spanish minister of the economy and deputy prime minister Rodrigo Rato is due to visit Bonn later on Wednesday.
Spain, Italy and Portugal are sometimes disparaged by northern European officials as the Club Med group, with high inflation, deficits and interest rates.

But Germany, one of the loudest advocates of a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria, is coming precariously close to missing the deficit goal. Over the weekend it raised its forecast for this year's deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP, after 3.9 percent last year.
Bonn has been saying EMU is likely to start in January 1999 with a small core group of participants.

German state secretary of finance Juergen Stark, without naming particular countries, on Tuesday said some aspirants should forsake the political prestige of joining EMU at the outset and wait until their economies are well enough prepared.
Aznar explicitly rejected such suggestions. "Impertinent remarks without a factual basis are easily made. But afterward one must deny them and write letters of apology," he said.
Spain must and will be among the founders of currency union, he said. "The citizens are prepared for that and the government is commited to doing everything necessary to achieve it."
Spain's commitment to the euro is more political than economic, as EMU is the way to the political integration of Europe, he said.
Germans fear the participation of the Club Med countries will soften the euro, making it vulnerable to inflation.
But Aznar said Spain wants a strong euro as much as Germany does, adding that he also opposes a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
"I know no Club Med. I know only one treaty, which sets certain entry conditions for all. And I am working to see we fulfil these conditions," he said.
